title: Observability Bootcamp & Triage Runbook for Inference Runtime
author: Priya R. Natarajan
content:
Overview:

This document is an onboarding-focused observability bootcamp and operational runbook for engineers and on-call SREs who will diagnose, triage, and mitigate production issues in the inference serving runtime. It distills the most common failure modes we see across kernel scheduling, KV cache, dispatch, and networked request surfaces and provides standard dashboards, playbooks, and example queries for pragmatic, repeatable investigations.

Audience:
- New runtime SREs and on-call engineers
- Backend engineers owning scheduler/kernel changes
- Applied ML engineers supporting model-onboarding incidents

Goals:
- Reduce mean time to detect (MTTD) and mean time to restore (MTTR) for runtime incidents
- Provide a repeatable cognitive checklist for triage across latency, correctness, and capacity classes
- Normalize telemetry and annotation conventions for rollouts and experiments

1) Quickstart: first 10 minutes on call
1.1 Triage checklist (prioritized):
1) Confirm alert context: alert name, fired time, route/model affected, severity, and any active rollout/experiment tags (see "Annotations & Tags" below).
2) Check global SLO dashboards (latency P50/P95/P99, error rate, per-route request rate) for correlated spikes.
3) Inspect kernel scheduler health panel for queue backlog and kernel backlog per-GPU.
4) Query trace samples for slow requests and check span breakdown (queue -> kernel dispatch -> inference -> postprocess).
5) If CPU/network saturation is suspected, inspect host-level metrics and network errors.

2) Observability primitives and conventions
- Service names: runtime-orch (orchestration), infer-gate (request ingress), kernel-gate (kernel manager), kvproxy (KV cache proxy), obs-collector (metrics/traces/log ingress).
- Alert naming convention: runtime.<component>.<symptom>.<severity> e.g., runtime.kernel-gate.queue-depth.critical
- Annotation keys (must be attached to requests and stored in trace attributes): rollout_id, variant (quantized|fp16|baseline), experiment, customer_tier, route_id.

3) Dashboards to open (ordered)
- Runtime: Global SLO Overview (P50/P95/P99, error budget burn)
- Kernel Scheduler: Per-GPU queue depth, kernel wait time, kernel dispatch rate, preemption count
- KV Cache: hit ratio (global & per-tenant), warmup rate, negative hit diffusion
- Network & IO: gRPC errors, connection churn, retransmits
- Cost & Throughput: tokens/sec, GPU utilization, model-replica counts

4) Standard queries and examples
4.1 PromQL examples (Grafana datasource):
- Per-route P95 latency (5m):
  
  histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(runtime_request_duration_seconds_bucket{route=~"$route"}[5m])) by (le))

- Kernel queue backlog (per GPU):
  
  sum(runtime_kernel_queue_depth) by (gpu_id)

- KV cache global hit ratio (1h window):
  
  sum(increase(kvproxy_hits_total[1h])) / sum(increase(kvproxy_requests_total[1h]))

4.2 Trace/Span patterns to look for (examples):
- Symptoms: long queue time with short kernel execution -> scheduler bottleneck
- Symptoms: long kernel execution and short queue time -> kernel optimization/degradation or wrong kernel variant
- Symptoms: high postprocess time -> downstream client or serialization issues

Example Jaeger-like span JSON snippet (single slow trace):
{
  "traceID": "abc123...",
  "spans": [
    {"operation": "ingest:parse", "duration_ms": 5},
    {"operation": "queue:kernel", "duration_ms": 450, "tags": {"gpu_id":"gpu-a12"}},
    {"operation": "kernel:forward", "duration_ms": 35, "tags": {"kernel_variant":"quant-fuse"}},
    {"operation": "postprocess:serialize", "duration_ms": 10}
  ]
}

5) Structured triage playbook (latency incident)
5.1 Step 0 — gather context
- Record incident ID, start time, alert thresholds
- Document active rollouts or quantization changes in the last 72 hours

5.2 Step 1 — isolate the layer
- If queue: queue depth and dispatch rate increased -> escalate to scheduler owners (kernel-scheduling team).
- If kernel: kernel execution time rose without queue increase -> collect recent kernel-release tags and CPU/GPU driver churn.
- If kvcache: hit ratio dropped -> check kvproxy error logs and cache warmup rate; examine recent model version swaps that invalidate prefixes.

5.3 Step 2 — quick mitigations (ordered by impact/risk)
1) Roll back recent kernel hint rollout (if annotated in traces and flagged in release chaperone).
2) Temporarily increase admission threshold for best-effort traffic and preserve reserved slots for SLO-critical routes. CLI example: 

  # Increase reserved slots for tiered routes (runtime-orch CLI)
  rdoctl admission update --tier critical --reserved-slots 30

3) Disable preemption for affected GPUs for 5–15 minutes if preemption churn correlates with latency spikes.
4) Enable shadow-routing of suspect route to a stable, lower-throughput model variant.

5.4 Step 3 — deep collection (when quick mitigations insufficient)
- Enable request-level debug sampling (increase trace sample rate to 100% for route-id X for 10 minutes).
- Collect full kernel traces: kernel_gcov, kernel_dispatch_profile, and executor logs from affected GPU hosts.
- Export recent microbenchmarks used by the scheduler for the current time window.

6) Runbook for error storms and connection churn
6.1 Symptoms: Sharp spike in gRPC UNAVAILABLE or connection resets
- Immediate checks: service endpoint health (kube probe), node-level TCP retransmits, ulimit of open files.
- Mitigation steps: temporarily shift traffic away from affected AZ/region, increase gRPC max-connections on fronting proxies, restart infer-gate pod after draining.

6.2 Example commands and logs to collect:
- Kubernetes pod status: kubectl -n runtime get pods -o wide --selector app=infer-gate
- Netstat summary: ss -s; ss -p | grep runtime-orch
- gRPC logged error snippet (example):
  
  E 2026-02-10T12:23:44.123Z infer-gate runtime: request failed: rpc error: code = Unavailable desc = connection closed by peer

7) Escalation matrix and ownership
- Level 1: On-call runtime SRE (primary) — initial triage and short mitigations (15–30m).
- Level 2: Kernel-scheduling owners / Inference runtime team — deep kernel and scheduler changes (30–120m).
- Level 3: Infra/Cloud/Networking — cross-host issues (120m+), driver or NVLink problems.

Contact roster (primary contact tags):
- runtime-oncall: #runtime-oncall in Slack
- kernel-scheduling: @kernel-sched-leads
- infra: #infra-ops

8) Post-incident follow-up checklist
- Create a postmortem within 72 hours for any incident > 3 hours or that breached an error budget.
- Include reproduction steps, top contributing causes, and a concrete remediation plan with owners and completion dates.
- Add instrumentation gaps found to the telemetry backlog and tag with "telemetry-gap".

9) Observability hygiene and instrumentation guidance (for PRs)
- Always add these trace attributes in request path: route_id, rollout_id, model_variant, request_priority.
- Use the standardized histogram buckets for request_duration_seconds (see table below).

Histogram buckets (recommended):
| bucket (s) | rationale |
|------------|-----------|
| 0.005 | parse/ingest micro-latency |
| 0.02  | fast responses |
| 0.1   | typical token-level requests |
| 0.5   | larger generation or batched flows |
| 2.0   | slow operations; investigate |
| 10.0  | gateway/backpressure expiry |

10) Example alert definitions (templates)
- kernel-gate.queue-depth.warning: runtime.kernel-gate.queue-depth.warning
  - Condition: sum(runtime_kernel_queue_depth) by (cluster) > 1000 for 5m
  - Runbook pointer: this doc -> section 5
- kvproxy.hitratio.critical
  - Condition: (sum(increase(kvproxy_hits_total[15m])) / sum(increase(kvproxy_requests_total[15m]))) < 0.5
  - Runbook pointer: section 5 & 6

11) Release and experiment annotation workflow (short)
- Before any kernel or scheduler hint rollout, create an experiment entry in the release tracker with an annotation token (e.g., rollout_id=rb-20260210-kh). The runtime orchestration will emit rollout_id on all traces so incidents can be correlated automatically.
- Toggle dark launches with runtime-orch feature flags and ensure the feature flag name is included as 'experiment' on traces.

12) Common debugging recipes (quick snippets)
A) Find top slowest routes in the last 15 minutes (PromQL):
  topk(10, histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(runtime_request_duration_seconds_bucket[15m])) by (le, route)))

B) Find hosts with highest kernel execution time per GPU: 
  topk(10, sum(runtime_kernel_exec_time_seconds) by (host, gpu_id))

C) Dump recent kvproxy error logs for tenant X: 
  rdoctl logs kvproxy --tenant X --since 30m --grep "ERR"

13) Appendix: instrumentation snippets and SDK examples
- OpenTelemetry span example (pseudocode):
  span = tracer.startSpan("kernel:forward")
  span.setAttribute("gpu_id", gpu_id)
  span.setAttribute("kernel_variant", "quant-fuse")
  span.end()

- Runtime-orch admission override example (YAML):
  apiVersion: runtime.redwood.ai/v1
  kind: AdmissionPolicy
  metadata:
    name: critical-reserved-slots
  spec:
    tier: critical
    reservedSlots: 30
    backoff: 10s

14) Ownership and maintenance cadence
- Owner: runtime-observability squad (rotating oncall: see team wiki for roster)
- Quarterly hygiene tasks:
  - Audit dashboards and remove unused panels
  - Validate alert thresholds against synthetic load profile
  - Run the observability runbook drill (game-day) once per quarter

15) Frequently seen root causes (historical examples)
- Kernel fingerprint regression after a fused-kernel rollout (fixed by rollback and kernel autotune).
- KV cache invalidation after model prefix change (mitigated by warming and routing tag).
- Preemption storms caused by mis-sized admission controller thresholds (fixed by adding hysteresis).

Related resources and links:
- Runtime telemetry sampling and cost playbook: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/runtime-telemetry-sampling-cost-aware-profiling-handbook-2027
- Kernel scheduling ADRs: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/scheduler-policy-language-declarative-profiles-2026
- On-call Slack channel: #runtime-oncall

If you are new on call, run the quickstart checklist at the top of this doc on every page load until you have handled 3 real incidents. That practice significantly reduces cognitive load during the first live incident.
